FrMS88-de7250-d1e111.summary: Poses the twentieth question: whether in via the intellect can know anything intuitively. Against: 'we see now through a glass darkly'.
claims: Paul's 'through a glass darkly' seems to deny intuitive knowledge in this life.

FrMS88-de7250-d1e122.summary: Contrary: 1 Corinthians, 'Who knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man that is in him?'
claims: The human spirit knows what is in it.

FrMS88-de7250-d1e127.summary: Announces a distinction of knowledge and then the answer. Knowledge is fourfold; the first is intuitive, which is of the thing through itself.
claims: Intuitive knowledge is of the thing through itself.

FrMS88-de7250-d1e136.summary: The second is abstractive, which is through a representative.
claims: Abstractive knowledge is through a representative.

FrMS88-de7250-d1e142.summary: The third is illative knowledge, of relations inferred from knowledge of their terms.
claims: Illative knowledge infers relations from knowledge of terms.

FrMS88-de7250-d1e149.summary: The fourth is discursive or argumentative, in two kinds: beginning from intuition and reaching what is not intuited (as knowledge of the intelligences starts from intuited motion), or beginning from abstraction and reaching what is not known abstractively (as substance and accidents). First conclusion: we know the act of understanding intuitively in via, since all experiential knowledge is intuitive (abstraction gives no experience of singulars), and we experience that we understand.
claims: Discursive knowledge begins from intuitive or abstractive knowledge and reaches what is not so known.
We know our act of understanding intuitively in this life.
All experiential knowledge is intuitive.

FrMS88-de7250-d1e191.summary: Second proof: any cognition by which something accidental in its object is known is intuitive, since a representative represents uniformly however accidents vary; and in knowing the act of understanding I know that it now inheres, which is accidental to it.
claims: Knowledge of accidental features is intuitive.

FrMS88-de7250-d1e204.summary: Third proof: no contingent truth can be known through a representative, which represents the same way however contingents vary; the truth that the act of understanding exists, its first contingent truth, is so known, hence intuitively.
claims: Contingent truths cannot be known through a representative.

FrMS88-de7250-d1e217.summary: Fourth proof: no contingent truth can be per se known except intuitively, since it is not per se known from its terms; 'the act exists' is known as per se known.
claims: Contingent truths are per se known only through intuition.

FrMS88-de7250-d1e226.summary: Second conclusion: nothing in the soul is known intuitively except acts. We argue to the soul's essence from its acts, to its powers likewise, to habits from signs in acts (ease of operation), and to species from knowing an act exists while the object is absent.
claims: Only the soul's acts are known intuitively; essence, powers, habits, and species are inferred.

FrMS88-de7250-d1e247.summary: All these are proved by one middle: nothing known precisely by discourse is known intuitively, and all these are known precisely by discourse.
claims: What is known only by discourse is not known intuitively.

FrMS88-de7250-d1e256.summary: Third conclusion: we know some things abstractively, since whatever is known directly and immediately while not existing is known abstractively, such as a non-existent rose.
claims: Non-existents, like a non-existent rose, are known abstractively.

FrMS88-de7250-d1e265.summary: Fourth conclusion: we know some things discursively, such as the soul's essence and its powers, per the second conclusion. First difficulty: our soul is as present to itself as its act of knowing, so it seems it should be equally known intuitively.
claims: The soul's essence and powers are known discursively.
Objection: the soul is as present to itself as its acts.

FrMS88-de7250-d1e278.summary: Reply: no formal cause can be assigned except that it is not known; but Augustine assigns an extrinsic cause for our ignorance of the soul's substance, namely the penalty of sin, by which the intellect cannot understand itself or the soul or other apprehensibles.
claims: Our ignorance of the soul's substance is a penalty of sin.

FrMS88-de7250-d1e291.summary: Second difficulty: whether the acts of other powers are known intuitively. Yes: otherwise no contingent truth about external things, such as the sun's motion, could be known with certainty; I know the heavens move because I know intuitively the act of the sensitive power terminated at this truth.
claims: The acts of other powers, including senses, are known intuitively.
Certainty about external contingents depends on intuiting our sensory acts.

FrMS88-de7250-d1e307.summary: Third difficulty: if intuitive cognition is perfect, why are so many questions disputed about the act (whether relative or absolute, etc.)? Reply: it is seen intuitively but not in every mode of knowledge, as sight sees the whole whiteness without discerning its specific difference.
claims: Intuitive knowledge of something need not grasp its specific nature.

FrMS88-de7250-d1e324.summary: Fourth difficulty: when things are essentially ordered, if the posterior is known so is the prior; many features of the act prior to its existence are unknown, so its existence would be more unknown. Reply: we know neither the act's proper notion nor its existence properly, but only in general that it exists. Adds that in intuitive knowledge the object functions as mover (relative to the power), cause or producer (relative to the act), measure (relative to habit and act), and terminus; in abstractive knowledge it need only terminate and measure.
claims: We know our act's existence only in general, not its proper nature.
In intuitive cognition the object moves, causes, measures, and terminates; in abstractive cognition only measures and terminates.

FrMS88-de7250-d1e357.summary: Reply to the opening argument: the Apostle speaks of the articles of faith.
claims: 'Through a glass darkly' refers to the articles of faith.

FrMS88-de7250.summary: The twentieth question of the prologue asks whether in this life (in via) the intellect can know anything intuitively. Meyronnes distinguishes four kinds of knowledge: intuitive (of the thing through itself), abstractive (through a representative), illative (of relations inferred from knowledge of terms), and discursive or argumentative, which either begins from intuition and reaches what is not intuited (as from motion to the intelligences) or begins from abstraction and reaches what is not known abstractively (as substance and accident). He then argues four conclusions: we know our act of understanding intuitively in this life, since it is known by experience, includes accidental and contingent features, and 'the act exists' is per se known though contingent; nothing in the soul except its acts is known intuitively — its essence, powers, habits, and species are inferred from acts; some things are known abstractively, such as a non-existent rose; and some, like the soul's essence and powers, discursively. He resolves four difficulties: Augustine attributes our ignorance of the soul's substance to the penalty of sin; the acts of the other powers, including the senses, are also known intuitively, which grounds certain knowledge of external contingents like the motion of the heavens; intuitive knowledge of an act need not grasp all of it, as sight sees whiteness without discerning its specific difference; and we know the act's existence only in general, not its proper nature. In intuitive knowledge the object functions as mover, cause, measure, and terminus; in abstractive, necessarily only as measure and terminus. Paul's 'through a glass darkly' concerns the articles of faith.
claims: Knowledge is intuitive, abstractive, illative, or discursive.
In this life we know our own act of understanding intuitively.
Nothing in the soul except its acts is known intuitively; the soul's essence, powers, habits, and species are inferred from acts.
Acts of the sensitive powers are known intuitively, grounding certain knowledge of external contingent truths.
Our ignorance of the soul's substance is, per Augustine, a penalty of sin.
In intuitive cognition the object moves, causes, measures, and terminates; in abstractive it need only measure and terminate.
